analysis.one_liner: Adds federal protections against abusive high-cost mortgage lending, while blocking states from setting stricter rules.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 48 bipartisan cosponsors after its April 2000 introduction but never received a subcommittee or floor vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tighten federal rules on high-cost mortgages: lower thresholds for when a loan counts as high-cost, limits on prepayment penalties and refinancing fees, a ban on creditors profiting from foreclosure sales, a ban on encouraging borrowers to default, and quarterly reporting of borrowers' payment histories to credit bureaus. At the same time, it would override state laws on the same subject and let Federal Reserve interpretations of state-law preemption have the force of law, and it would relax some disclosures, including how mortgage brokers are paid by lenders.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers taking high-cost loans against their homes, who would get tighter definitions of abusive loans, limits on fees that strip home equity, a ban on creditors profiting from foreclosures, and a faster right to a payoff statement when refinancing or resolving a default [S2] [S3]. Mortgage brokers would also gain clarity that they can be paid by lenders as well as borrowers [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Lowers the interest-rate and points-and-fees thresholds that define a high-cost mortgage (from 10 percentage points to 8 or 9, and from 8 percent to 6 or 7), bringing more loans under federal protection [S2] [S3].
Caps prepayment penalties on a declining schedule (3%, then 2%, then 1% of the loan amount) and shortens the period they can apply from five years to three [S3].

Bars a creditor from making a high-cost refinance within a year of an existing high-cost loan unless fees are charged only on new money advanced or the rate drops by at least two points, a curb on repeated fee-stripping refinancings [S3].

Prohibits creditors from profiting from the foreclosure sale of the property, from advising a consumer to skip payments on existing debts, and from mandatory prepayment of funds; also limits closing costs [S2] [S3].

Requires creditors to report both favorable and unfavorable payment history to a nationally recognized credit bureau at least quarterly, and to provide a payoff statement within three business days of a request [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-cost mortgage lenders and brokers, who would face tighter loan definitions, fee limits, a ban on foreclosure profits, and new reporting and payoff-statement duties [S2] [S3]. State governments would also lose authority to set stricter rules than the federal ones [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would preempt state laws on the same subject, including state limits on high-cost and high-fee loans, and Federal Reserve interpretations of that preemption would have the effect of law, which could replace stricter state protections with the weaker federal floor [S3].
It would repeal existing disclosure requirements for prepayment penalties while revising which penalties are permitted, reducing the information borrowers receive at closing [S2].

It would amend the standard settlement-cost form so it no longer must itemize fees that settlement providers earn but that are paid by the lender, and would require only a booklet explanation that brokers can be compensated with lender-paid funds, making broker compensation less visible on the form itself [S3].
It would redraw creditor liability guidelines for disclosure errors, replacing the existing statutory liability framework with cure-based remedies for creditors who fix mistakes [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The substantive protections are real: more loans covered, fee-stripping refinancings curbed, foreclosure profits banned, and payment histories reported so borrowers can build credit. But the bill pairs those gains with broad federal preemption of state law and Federal Reserve interpretations carrying the force of law, and with softer disclosure of how brokers are compensated. Whether borrowers come out ahead would depend heavily on whether state rules were stricter than the new federal ones — exactly what the bill would prevent states from maintaining.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking Committee and two of its subcommittees on the day it was introduced, and no further action ever came before the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Ney introduced the bill in the House on April 6, 2000 [S1] [S5].

The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services and to its Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit and Subcommittee on Housing and Community Opportunity [S5].
No further action — no markup, no committee or floor vote — appears in the action history before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].
The bill attracted 48 cosponsors, 37 Republicans and 11 Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost mortgage lenders kept operating under the existing rules, avoiding the new fee limits, foreclosure-profit ban, and reporting duties. Consumers also kept whatever stricter state protections existed, since the bill's federal preemption never passed; the disclosure and broker-compensation relaxations died with it. Because the bill mixed protections with preemption, the death of the bill cut both ways, and the status quo of state-by-state rules survived.

against.name: House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Took no further action after the April 6, 2000 referral; the bill never reached a markup or a floor vote

against.name: Consumer and community groups opposed to federal preemption of state anti-predatory-lending laws
against.what_they_did: Opposed preemption-based mortgage bills of this type, arguing a federal floor would displace stricter state rules

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 37 Republicans and 11 Democrats — but no vote ever occurred, so the vote split is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would tighten the definition of high-cost loans, cap fees and prepayment penalties, ban foreclosure profits, and require quarterly credit reporting. But its federal preemption would bar states from setting stricter rules, and Federal Reserve interpretations would carry the force of law — a structure that can lock in a federal floor where state standards were tougher, which is why the industry's core interest here runs against the strongest available protections. [S2] [S3]

The RESPA amendments would stop requiring the settlement form to itemize lender-paid fees and would formally acknowledge broker compensation funded by lenders, a practice that raises borrower costs through higher loan pricing. Borrowers would learn of it only in an information booklet. [S3]

Creditors would be required to report mortgage payment histories to a nationally recognized bureau at least quarterly, sending more data to bureaus while helping borrowers with thin credit files build a record. [S3]
